scenes.title: The problem: an anomaly is not an answer
scenes.subtitle: Course 101's assistant can tell you the AMF looks anomalous. But a network operations team needs the why — a root-cause report backed by evidence, where every claim points to a specific log or metric record. Ungrounded assertions from a language model are worse than useless in a NOC; they're a liability. So how do we get an agent to investigate, and then prove its work?
scenes.say: In course one-oh-one we built an assistant that can tell you the A M F looks anomalous. But an anomaly is not an answer. A network operations team needs the why — a root-cause report, backed by evidence, where every single claim points to a specific log or metric record. An ungrounded assertion from a language model, confidently stated but unsupported, is worse than useless in a live network operations center; it is a liability. So the problem for course two-oh-one is this: how do we get an agent to genuinely investigate an incident, and then prove its work? Let's build it.

scenes.tab: Develop & train · Experiments — the agent-school courses, live
scenes.caption: Every course is a real, tracked experiment on our DevOps cluster called Rome. 201-rca-investigator is where the root-cause agent's work is recorded.
scenes.say: First, some orientation. Everything in this series runs for real on our DevOps cluster called Rome, and each course is a tracked experiment you can see right here in the OpenShift A I dashboard. The one we care about now is two-oh-one, the R C A investigator. Unlike the classic machine-learning courses, this agent's work is not a training run — it is a set of traces, because the substance of this course is a reasoning agent, and what we track is how it reasons.

scenes.tab: Solution shape — a two-phase agent over a retrieval service
scenes.caption: An ephemeral two-phase agent (investigate → write) over a separately-deployed RAG service. The same vLLM serves the agent and its judge; MLflow receives both the traces and the verdicts.
scenes.say: Here is the shape of the solution. The agent is an ephemeral job with two phases. In the investigate phase it retrieves correlated logs and metrics; in the write phase it composes the analysis. Crucially, the search index it depends on does not live inside the agent — it is a separately deployed retrieval service, the R A G backend, so re-indexing or swapping retrievers never touches the agent. That is the pattern-two lesson. One more elegant detail: the very same v L L M endpoint that powers the agent's reasoning also powers the judge that grades it afterward, and M L flow receives both the agent's traces and the judge's verdicts. Quality is measured on the same platform, with the same model, no external grading service. Now let's watch it work.

scenes.tab: GenAI · Observability overview — traces, latency, tokens
scenes.caption: No bespoke telemetry code: mlflow.openai.autolog() plus the workspace shim turns every LLM call into a trace — 17 traces, 2.32s latency, zero errors, full token accounting.
scenes.say: The agent needs almost no observability code of its own. One line — m l flow's OpenAI autolog — plus the workspace shim, and every single language-model call becomes a trace. This is the GenAI overview for the investigator on our DevOps cluster called Rome: seventeen traces, an average latency of two-point-three seconds, a zero-percent error rate, and full token accounting — nearly forty-seven thousand tokens across the run. This is what it means to treat an agent as a first-class, observable workload: you get the operational picture for free.

scenes.tab: GenAI · Traces — the two-phase economics, visible
scenes.caption: The trace list shows the cost-aware routing directly: many small investigate calls (297, 1144, 2224 tokens) and one large, cited write-up (3760 tokens).
scenes.say: And the trace list shows the economics of the design directly. Read the token counts down the right side. There are many small investigate calls — two hundred, a thousand, two thousand tokens — as the agent gathers evidence cheaply. And then there is one large call, thirty-seven hundred tokens, that produces the finished, cited root-cause analysis. That is cost-aware model routing inside a single agent task: spend little to investigate, spend more only to write the one thing that matters. You are seeing the agent's strategy, not just its output.

scenes.tab: GenAI · Trace detail — the evidence-grounding judge verdict
scenes.caption: The write-up trace carries its judge verdict as an assessment. The system prompt forces citations; the 'evidence-grounding' judge (on the cluster's own Kimi) scores whether it obeyed.
scenes.say: Now open that write-up trace, and here is the heart of course two-oh-one. On the left, the system prompt is uncompromising: use only the evidence records provided, and every factual claim must cite a record id in brackets. On the right, in the Assessments panel, is the verdict — the evidence-grounding judge, running on the cluster's own Kimi model, has scored this report. A cited report scores yes; a tool-loop trace with no report scores no. Evidence discipline is not a hope pinned to a prompt; it is measured, on the trace, by the platform. Ungrounded sentences become visible bugs — exactly what a network operations team needs before it trusts a machine's root-cause.

scenes.title: 201, solved: the agent investigates, and proves it
scenes.subtitle: RAG as a skill backend, cost-aware routing inside one task, and evidence-grounding measured as platform data — the judge verdict lives on the very trace it scores, produced by the same model the agent uses. Next: 202 moves from investigation to a full train-and-serve classic-ML pipeline for fraud triage.
scenes.say: So that's two-oh-one, solved. The agent investigates an incident using retrieval as a proper skill backend, routes its spending intelligently within a single task, and — most importantly — proves its work, with an evidence-grounding judge whose verdict lives on the very trace it scores, produced by the same model the agent itself uses. No external grader, no unverified claims. From here, course two-oh-two moves from investigation to production: a full train-and-serve classic machine-learning pipeline for fraud triage. Thanks for watching.
